title: Rice is Nice
summary: Hosts Josh and Chuck (with the transcript's "iHeart Intro" label on Chuck's lines) explore rice as a food: that rice is a seed/cereal, white vs. brown rice and enrichment methods, rice types (basmati, jasmine, sushi, sticky, arborio/carnaroli, bomba, Carolina gold, black, wild rice), rice history and cultivation in flooded paddies and upland farming, environmental costs (methane, nitrous oxide, water use) and fish-rice farming, arsenic contamination concerns, top rice producing and consuming countries, and rice dishes and desserts (jollof, biryani, paella, sushi, rice pudding, mochi, horchata). Closes with a listener mail from Ted about finishing the full catalog.

segments.title: Opening banter and rice's global importance
segments.summary: Hosts open with banter about the episode topic and note rice's role as a staple food, calories consumed worldwide, and rice production supporting households in developing countries.

segments.title: Rice as a seed and enrichment
segments.summary: Rice is explained as the seed of the rice plant, classified as a cereal. White rice is described as brown rice with bran and germ removed, and the hosts describe enrichment methods such as powder-coating select grains and mixing them back in, layered coatings, and extruded fake grains.

segments.title: Rice origins and subspecies
segments.summary: Rice descends from Oryza sativa domesticated in China, with Indica and Japonica subspecies differing in grain length and starch (amylopectin vs amylose). African rice, Oryza glaberrima, is discussed as hardier, with the idea of crossbreeding the two.

segments.title: Basmati, jasmine, sushi, and sticky rice
segments.summary: The hosts discuss basmati, jasmine (whose scent is natural), sushi rice (a japonica treated with vinegar, salt, and sugar), and sticky or glutinous rice, which is sticky due to high amylopectin and is not gluten-containing.

segments.title: Risotto and paella rices
segments.summary: Arborio and carnaroli are named as medium-grain japonica rices for risotto, which requires constant stirring. Bomba rice for paella is discussed, noting it should not be substituted with other short-grain rices.

segments.title: Cooking anecdotes
segments.summary: Brief banter about making paella at home, with a joke about a cooking show featuring Gwyneth Paltrow.

segments.title: Carolina gold and other varieties
segments.summary: Carolina gold is described as a heirloom long-grain japonica from the Carolina lowlands, reportedly brought to Charleston from Madagascar in the 1600s, lost after the Civil War, and revived in the 1990s by Anson Mills. Enslaved Africans' knowledge of wetland rice cultivation is discussed. Black rice (forbidden rice) and wild rice (not a true rice) are also covered.

segments.title: Rice history and paddy cultivation
segments.summary: Rice cultivation is traced to the Yangtze River basin in China, spreading to South Asia and Southeast Asia. Lowland flooded paddies and upland terraced farming are compared, with notes on irrigation and draining for harvest.

segments.title: Growing and harvesting rice
segments.summary: Methods of growing rice are described, including nursery beds, transplanting, seed drilling, and air-dropping seed, with roughly 120 days to grow. Traditional handsickle harvesting produces rough rice, which is hulled to brown rice.

segments.title: Milling white rice
segments.summary: Milling removes the bran to produce white rice; some rice is polished, sometimes with glucose, and may then be enriched.

segments.title: Rice environmental impact and fish-rice farming
segments.summary: Rice's water use is discussed relative to other crops, with California rice production noted. Flooded paddies produce methane; draining reduces methane but increases nitrous oxide. Rice-fish farming is described as reducing methane and pests, increasing yields, and reducing fertilizer needs. Growing rice in seawater is mentioned as an research effort.

segments.title: Arsenic in rice
segments.summary: Rice absorbs arsenic more than most crops, and arsenic concentrates in bran and germ, so brown rice has more. A 2023 Frontiers in Nutrition article is cited as calling for more study. Consumer Reports testing is referenced; California rice is suggested as lower in arsenic. Rinsing and cooking in excess water are suggested to reduce it, and children and daily consumers are noted as at risk.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break before the production statistics segment.

segments.title: Rice production by country and US rice
segments.summary: Asia is the top rice producing continent, with China first, then India and Bangladesh; all top ten producers are Asian. US rice is produced mainly in California, Louisiana, Texas, Mississippi, Missouri, and Arkansas, with about 80 percent of US rice eaten being domestic.

segments.title: Rice consumption by country and rice in childhood
segments.summary: China and India are the top consumers by population; Bangladesh leads per capita at about 592 pounds of dry rice per year, with Nigeria in the top ten. The hosts link high consumption to lower income and developing economies. A childhood school lunch of plain rice is recalled, and a Tottori University study on falling rice consumption as wealth grows is mentioned.

segments.title: Rice dishes worldwide
segments.summary: Jollof rice, biryani, and paella are discussed as rice dishes. The hosts mention preferences for Indian curries like tikka masala and butter chicken, and Japanese chicken katsu.

segments.title: Sushi origins and paella origins
segments.summary: Paella is described as a Spanish dish with clam juice flavoring, and clamato is mentioned. Sushi's origins in vinegar-preserved fish are discussed, including nare sushi.

segments.title: Rice desserts and drinks
segments.summary: Rice pudding, ube condensed milk, mango sticky rice, Polish rice cake, mochi (including the rabbit-in-the-moon tradition), and horchata made from rice soaked in evaporated milk are discussed.

segments.title: Horchata recipe and snack chatter
segments.summary: Hosts encourage making horchata at home with about five or six ingredients. Chuck discusses cherry frosted pop tarts.

segments.title: Listener mail from Ted
segments.summary: Ted writes that he has finished the full Stuff You Should Know catalog for the fifth time and lists what he likes: the hosts' character arcs over seventeen years, not talking over each other, learning about movies and music, and an in-joke about never finishing a list. Hosts thank Ted and invite listener email.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts give the email address for listener mail and the iHeartRadio credit.
